title: Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica from a Nerve Root)
case: Case: A 45-year-old man has 10 days of right leg pain down the back of the leg to the outer foot. Back pain is mild. Right calf raises are weaker (4 out of 5) and the right Achilles reflex is reduced. SLR reproduces leg pain at about 40 degrees and neck flexion increases it. No saddle numbness, no bladder or bowel change. Prone press-ups centralise the pain.
Working diagnosis: right S1 radiculopathy, likely disc-related. Plan: education, press-ups, walking, neural sliders if calm, calf strengthening, weekly neurological reassessment.
plan: education, press-ups, walking, neural sliders if calm, calf strengthening, weekly neurological reassessment.

differentials.name: Cauda equina syndrome
differentials.key: Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, bilateral signs

differentials.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis
differentials.key: Older, walking-related leg symptoms, eased by sitting

differentials.name: Peroneal nerve palsy
differentials.key: Foot drop with sensory loss at the lateral leg, pressure at the fibular head

differentials.name: Vascular claudication
differentials.key: Calf pain with walking, relieved by standing, weak pulses

qa: Why test calf raises and the Achilles reflex? They are the main clues to the S1 root, so they help locate the level and track recovery.
The patient reports numbness in the saddle area. What do you do? Stop, treat as suspected cauda equina syndrome and arrange emergency hospital referral at once.
Why does neck flexion increase leg pain in the SLR? It adds tension through the nervous system, which suggests neural sensitivity. It does not prove a particular structure.
Leg pain spreads below the knee during press-ups. What do you do? Stop, because symptoms are peripheralising. Try another direction or modify.
Why is traction not the main treatment? Evidence shows little added benefit, and active strategies are better supported.

fields.Purpose: Check whether stretching the sciatic nerve path reproduces the leg pain, suggesting nerve root irritation (especially L5 and S1)
fields.Therapist position: At the side of the symptomatic leg, one hand under the heel, the other on the knee to keep it straight
fields.Action: Slowly lift the straight leg by flexing the hip, with the knee fully extended and the ankle relaxed. Note the angle at which leg pain starts
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the patient's usual leg pain radiating below the knee, usually between about 30 and 70 degrees of hip flexion [Ref - to verify the exact angle range]. Stretch behind the thigh only is not positive
fields.Sensitising step: At the angle just below symptom onset, add ankle dorsiflexion or neck flexion. Increased leg pain supports a neural cause; release it to see if pain falls
fields.Supports: A positive result supports a lumbar nerve root cause. SLR is reported to be sensitive but not specific, so a negative test makes disc herniation less likely but does not exclude other root causes [Ref - to verify]
fields.Errors: Rotating the leg; bending the knee; stopping when hamstring tightness appears; counting back pain only
fields.Next step: If positive, do the crossed SLR and slump test

fields.Action: Lift the unaffected leg using the same method
fields.Positive: Reproduces pain in the affected leg
fields.Supports: Reported to be more specific for disc herniation but less often present [Ref - to verify]

fields.Patient position: Sitting at the edge of the bench, hands behind the back, thighs supported
fields.Action (in order): 1) Slump the trunk. 2) Flex the neck. 3) Extend the knee. 4) Dorsiflex the ankle. Stop when symptoms reproduce
fields.Differentiation: Release the neck flexion. If the symptoms reduce, it suggests neural tension
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the patient's leg symptoms, which change with neck position
fields.Negative: No reproduction, or normal symmetrical stretch sensations
fields.Supports: Neural mechanosensitivity, not a specific lesion

fields.Use: Anterior thigh pain, suspected upper lumbar roots (L2-L4)
fields.Action: Passively flex the knee, adding hip extension if needed

redFlags.Finding: Saddle numbness, new urinary retention or incontinence, bowel change, sexual dysfunction
redFlags.Immediate action: Stop; same-day hospital emergency referral; do not delay for further tests

redFlags.Finding: Rapidly progressive or severe weakness (for example foot drop worsening within days)
Severe unremitting pain not helped by any position
redFlags.Why it matters: Serious pathology or severe nerve irritation

manual.name: Neural mobilization (sliders)
manual.why: May reduce neural mechanosensitivity [Ref - to verify]
manual.finding: Positive SLR or slump, not severely irritable
manual.application: Lying or sitting; move knee extension and ankle plantar flexion together, then reverse; gentle, 5 to 10 reps
manual.stop: Symptoms last longer than a short time after

manual.name: Lumbar mobilization guided by symptom response
manual.application: Prone press-ups or side-glide, gentle graded oscillations
manual.stop: Symptoms spread further down the leg

manual.name: Thoracic and hip mobilization
manual.why: Reduces stiffness that adds load to the lumbar spine

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education, directional-preference exercise if found, and walking. Manual therapy is optional and mainly for short-term relief. Avoid high-velocity manipulation when there is a significant neurological deficit. Evidence for manual therapy in radiculopathy is limited [Ref - to verify].
Is it working? Better leg pain, symptoms moving toward the spine, higher SLR angle and improved function.

exercise.Starting dose: 5 to 10 minutes, several times a day

exercise.Exercise: Directional preference movement (e.g. prone press-up or standing extension)
exercise.Steps: Repeat 10 reps a few times a day
Lying on the back, hold the thigh, alternate knee extension with ankle plantar flexion, then reverse
Hands on thighs, push hips back with a neutral spine

exercise.Exercise: Graded strength (squat, deadlift pattern, calf raise)
exercise.Objective: Return to function and rebuild lost strength

exerciseNotes: If there is weakness, add specific strengthening for the weak muscle group (for example calf raises for S1, heel walks and band dorsiflexion for L4-L5) as tolerated.

modalities.name: Mechanical traction
modalities.comment: Evidence shows little added benefit [Ref - to verify]

pathway: Rapidly progressive motor loss? Yes: urgent same-day review.
Leg-dominant pain below the knee, root-pattern signs and a positive neural tension test? Yes: working diagnosis is lumbar radiculopathy.
Mild or stable deficit? Yes: begin conservative care and monitor. No: refer urgently while supporting the patient.

Supports: below-knee pain, matching root signs, positive SLR or slump. Argues against: pain only in the back or buttock, normal neurological exam, no nerve tension signs. Must not miss: cauda equina syndrome, infection, tumour.
Visit 1: screen carefully, examine, explain that most radicular pain improves with time.
Early: calm symptoms, keep moving, find a directional preference, advise on positions.
Middle: add strength and function work; build tolerance to sitting, driving and lifting.
